“O death, I will be your death; O hell, I will be your bite.”
From the Lauds of Holy Saturday.
My love for the old images of the Crucifixion.
For example: the fish Remora; the mention of Pan, who enters into no marriage and marries only his own Echo; the idola specus, the idols of the cave; and so on.
Important for Shakespeare and for Hobbes, who appears to lack this mythic sense completely—but who probably only suppressed it consistently, since the Leviathan is itself one enormous mythic image.
How strange that Hobbes did not emerge in public until he was already a mature man.

What was going on inside him when he was young? But let us stay with Pan, who can marry only his own Echo. This is a symbol of post-Christian paganism returning to nature, of Goethean humanism, indeed of the whole German ideal of Bildung, insofar as it is aesthetically defined.
All the efforts of these ego-armored connoisseurs end in marriage to their own echo.
Why does G. F. Jünger omit this detail from his otherwise magnificent portrait of Pan?
Why does he forget Pan’s marriage to his own Echo?
Ah—but what drives these discoverers of Pan is only cultivated learning, not true panic terror.
The ego too can marry only its own echo. It is incapable of any other marriage. It is equally incapable of any other property—and of possessing its own grave.
Marriage and property are both, for the ego, phenomena belonging to das Man, the anonymous “they.”
Now listen carefully to this sentence from Martin Heidegger:
“The They-self says ‘I—I’ most loudly and most frequently because, at bottom, it is not authentically itself and evades its own authentic potentiality-for-Being.”
The magnificently desperate power of abstraction in Thomas Hobbes.
His desperate vis superba formae, the proud power of form, in the nominalist concept.
Conceptual power of the highest kind. These are the great jurists of the age, just as Kepler and Galileo are its great physicists.
J. Vialatoux is merely an apologist. He drives everyone else into the dead end of an either-or and then presents himself as the victor with “Love.”
In that case, give me Hobbes.
Bodin’s own view must still be established.
Let us jurists be silent about ourselves.

“From the social and ecclesiastical dreams active in the lives of the peasants, spiritualists, Anabaptists, and Savonarola (!) there runs a line of connection to the political novels of Thomas More and Campanella.”

You can forgive a good man like Robert Mohl for using a phrase such as “political novels,” but not Wilhelm Dilthey. He ought to have defined exactly the nature of the novel and of the novelistic: the journey of a problematic individual toward himself.
G. Lukács, Theory of the Novel, p. 75.
Irony toward the realization of the ideal.
The element of irony is very strong in some utopias, for example Samuel Butler’s Erewhon.
In Campanella it is completely absent.
In Samuel Butler it is strongly biographical and is therefore, in that respect too, more genuinely a novel.
Erewhon is a utopian novel, not a pure utopia.
The irony and humor in More, Butler, and Huxley are English additions, not the essence of utopia itself.
The English, as individuals, are incapable of a pure and unconditional utopia because they are incapable of surrendering themselves unconditionally to a collective order simply as such.
For them utopia is a vehicle for criticism of the age, irony, and so on. For the French utopians, it is bitterly serious and polemical.
Today suicide contains a renunciation of the grave.
Or, to put it the other way around: it is a conclusion drawn from the realization that the grave has been taken from us, that we no longer have a grave.

What is the structure of the thing that can be protected or attacked by such a crime, when the crime is defined not through a precise description of an act but exclusively through its general hideousness?

The end of the younger Masaryk affects me deeply and completely personally, at that point within private life where the existential contact takes place between the great whole and the individual human being placed at the disposal of the World Spirit.
With Masaryk’s suicide, the European age in which one could choose between West and East comes to an end.
The elder Masaryk had been a true European katechon, a restraining force: the katechon of Western liberal democracy.

With an astonishing degree of historical consciousness—infinitely greater than anything the German politicians, philosophers, or historians of the time could summon—old Masaryk chose the West after the most thorough reflection. He knew Russia and the East better than most Germans, Poles, or Serbs of his time. He loved that Russia. But his intellectual decision was for the West. He married an American woman, and that marriage became a symbol larger than their private lives: the symbol of his choice of the West.

The son born from that marriage, who has now killed himself in Prague, was the guarantor of that Western choice, together with Beneš, whom Masaryk had designated as his successor. And so this age now ends with the son throwing himself from a window of the Czernin Palace. This is more than the earlier Defenestrations of Prague: that of the New Town councillors in 1419, and that of the imperial councillors in May 1618. This is the Czechs’ own suicidal fall from the window, following the fall of the Germans and the many suicides of April 1945.
What wars will this third Defenestration of Prague set in motion?

I feel that this is one of those moments in my life when the personally private and the all-encompassing universal meaning of events coincide, and when God’s ordering shadow touches my small individual life.
I must tell my daughter this so that I have a witness.
